eyebrow: Search for Common Ground · every horizontal shoot, 2024–2026 · Instagram Feature (90 min, 16:9)
title: Imagine If:
headline: People with every reason to hate each other choose to sit in the same room. Ninety minutes, from a New York park path to South Sudan, Freetown, Sweida, Kërçova, Doha and Nairobi: what happens in the space between two sides?
story: Instagram now takes 90-minute horizontal videos ("Features"), and Kalindi asked where our head is at. This is the answer: one film made from every horizontal frame we have shot for Search since 2024. It opens on a line nobody forgets: we make peace with enemies, we don't make peace with friends. Then it asks two questions. Why would anyone sit down with their enemy? And can that work when people are really being killed?

Eight chapters answer them, each one a story that also works on its own as a Reel: strangers on a New York park path holding a tin can string, an Irish childhood on the border with the enemy at the kitchen table, a South African truth commission, a Palestinian mother and an Israeli woman who lost her brother, side by side, peacebuilders in South Sudan, Sierra Leone, Syria and Nairobi, children learning two languages in Kërçova, neighbours at Gatherings across America. It ends where it started, in the park, with balloons going up and one word: space. The film is the long-form home of Imagine If and the $100K match.
do: Open on Aida mid-line at 0:00. No logo, title or fade.
Name super on each person's first sync; place super when we land somewhere new.
Let it breathe: a tin can, balloon or b-roll breather every 3–5 minutes.
Cut every line from the raw camera file. Finished edits are reference only.
Grade every shoot to one warm, natural look before export.
dont: Never put SFCG, CGLA, CGL, "Academy" or Preemptive Love on screen.
No animation inside a chapter, no camera-shutter sounds, no freeze frames.
Never show program participants from Palestine or Afghanistan. Hidden faces stay hidden.
No stock, news or archive clips (rights). Skip the AP archive in the Kërçova edit.
Don't let one speaker take over a chapter.

Brussels: Sony FX6 3840×2160 25p, 4 mono tracks. New York 2026: Sony FX9 MXF 16:9, 23.976 fps, MIC voices as separate MP3. Doha: FX6 1920×1080 25p S-Cinetone. Kërçova: A7 IV 3840×2160 23.98p. Ramallah: A7S III 3840×2160 50p S-Log3. Kenya 2024: A7 III 3840×2160 25p HLG. South Sudan: Canon C70 4K. Sierra Leone: proxies only (no full-res found).
25p and 50p interviews: frame sampling, never optical flow on faces. 50p b-roll can play at 40% speed for slow motion.
One warm, natural look across every shoot before export (S-Log3 and HLG need their LUTs). New York: Kalindi's "noise of the city" look. Never export ungraded.
Use the lav channel on interviews (check per clip). Natural sound under every breather. Mix −14 LUFS integrated, −1 dBTP. Music 6–8 dB under voices.

Epidemic Sound only (an Envato track once caused a YouTube claim on Search). Shortlist from the licensed catalogue, one bed per chapter; swap freely inside Epidemic Sound:
• Cold open + title: Threads (Ever So Blue), solo piano, hopeful.
• Ch 1 New York: Between Two Pines (Erik Fernholm), light acoustic; has stems, so drop the drums under voices. Alt: Campfire Blues (Erik Fernholm).
• Ch 2–3 Brussels: Grandma's Piano (Franz Gordon), Oaks and Willows (Anna Landström), Les Artistes (Eva Hummingbird). Low, never under a key line.
• Ch 4 Pain Is Pain: Elan (Fabien Tell), small ensemble; Rhapsodic Sprout (Rand Aldo) for the Laila + Ayelet return.
• Interlude: no music under the phone voices; Cradle (Ever So Blue) only as the tail.
• Ch 5 On the Ground: Trace (Lennon Hutton), soft pulse for the map jumps, melody stem only under voices.
• Ch 6 The Next Table: Morgontimma (Christian Nanzell), hopeful folk.
• Ch 7 At Home: That's Fine (Instrumental Version) (Nashional), warm acoustic.
• Ch 8 finale: Nascency (Christoffer Moe Ditlevsen) builds into the balloon release; music fully out for Courtney's song; I Will Love You To The End (Johannes Bornlöf) under the last minute and the end card.
Burned in on every spoken line, all languages subtitled into English. Look: open decision (see Open decisions).
Master ProRes 422 HQ 1920×1080. Instagram: H.264 1920×1080, high bitrate, one file. Also export each chapter as its own file for Reels cut-downs.
checklist: Frame 1 is Aida mid-line. No logo, title, card or fade at 0:00.
Every name super matches the spelling in the client file (Hélène Calame with accents; Siham Fayyad with two y's; Kërçova with ë and ç).
Nowhere on screen: SFCG, CGLA, CGL, "Academy", Preemptive Love. North Macedonia super says Center for Common Ground.
Every spoken line is cut from the RAW camera file, not from a finished edit.
No program participants from Palestine or Afghanistan; hidden faces stay hidden.
No freeze frames anywhere. No camera-shutter sounds. No animation inside a chapter except the listed graphics.

Chapter cards show the right chapter number and the 8-step progress bar.

decisions.b: Imagine If (recommended: it is the live campaign name, so the film, the Reels and the donation page all match). Other options: The Space in Between (Courtney and the tin can) or We Make Peace With Enemies (Aida's line). "90 Minutes of Common Ground" and "The Space Between Us" are already used by other Search videos.

Two looks exist: the blue #1E6FD6 box (Search's social videos) and the semi-transparent dark bar (Search's long-form videos). Recommended: the dark bar for the 90-minute film, because it is easier on the eye for a long watch, and the blue box on the chapter Reels.

Plan: one 90-minute Instagram Feature on Search's account, with each chapter cut as a Reel that links to it. If Features is not yet switched on for Search's account, post the chapters as an Instagram Series and the full film on YouTube.

decisions.t: End card: match or no match
decisions.b: Export two versions of the last 10 seconds: one with "Every gift is doubled, up to $100,000." for while the Imagine If match is live, and one without it for after.

Search asked that Israel/Palestine lines from Brussels only use lines already in the approved shorts. New lines in this plan, all flagged in the script: Nadav (Chapter 3, two rows; he also names J Street in the same interview, which is not used), Maya and Rami in Doha (Chapter 4), Laila and Ayelet lines beyond the approved short (Chapter 4, about grief and listening only), and Siham and Hakeem in Nairobi (staff, about hope). None of them blames a side.

decisions.t: Brussels shorts still waiting for Search
decisions.b: Several Brussels lines in this film also appear in the Brussels shorts that are still with Search for approval. Any change Search makes there should carry over to this film.

Rami's surname: the super uses Rami Assali as in Search's glossary (the "Al-" prefix is still unconfirmed; the burned-in "Rami Asri" in the Doha edit is wrong). Nadav has a first-name super only until his title is confirmed.

Courtney sings live into the tin can for about 40 seconds. The transcript has no words, so we don't know the song yet. If it is a public-domain aria or a wordless line, it is clear. If it is a copyrighted song, Instagram may mute the film, so it needs a licence or a much shorter cut. The approved short "Courtney sings" has the same question.

In the 2025 Washington Square Park footage, Kalindi greets Hannah like a stranger (764_2756). Later in the day she calls her "my coworker, Hannah" (764_2767 at 05:59). The film never presents a coworker as a stranger. Hannah's rows are flagged and can come out as one block if she is staff.

Some frames in this plan come from finished edits and still show their burned-in captions (tagged "use raw"), and some in/out times are estimated inside long transcript paragraphs. An overnight pass on the raw camera files replaces those frames with clean ones, confirms every in/out point and builds a first test cut. The one thing that unlocks it: give this Claude session access to the footage folders on the Mac Studio (the home folder and the Library drive).

client_note: Why this matters: Instagram just opened 90-minute Features. Search already has the footage; this film turns three years of shoots into one piece that carries the Imagine If match, and its chapters become the campaign's Reels.

chapters.title: Cold open
chapters.line: Opens on the film's strongest line, plants both questions and closes the first at once. Then it shows the faces of the film from four corners of the world, names the stakes (65 conflicts, the most since 1946), lets two people say what this work can cost, and lands the title.

chapters.title: Are we related?
chapters.line: The problem at street level. Strangers in New York say why common ground feels harder now: we form groups, algorithms show us what we already think, people pass each other by. The first hints of an answer come from the same strangers: connection, one person who listens, and the time to think.

chapters.title: Before the Peace
chapters.line: The film lands in Brussels and meets people who built peace before any agreement existed. Gina and Paddy show how ordinary people in Northern Ireland made the Good Friday Agreement possible and then held it together; Christos shows the same idea with young Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots who had never met. It ends on the past that still has to be faced, which opens Chapter 3.

chapters.title: Read the Page
chapters.line: Chapter 2 ended on a past that still has to be faced. Here Hayley explains how South Africa's Truth Commission made denial impossible, and why truth alone is not enough. Youssef, a retired diplomat, admits governments did not listen to civil society; Aida and Nadav say people can work together without agreeing on everything. It ends on people who are hurt and still show up, which opens Chapter 4.

chapters.title: Pain Is Pain
chapters.line: Chapter 3 ended on people who are hurt and still show up. Here we meet them: Ahmad from Afghanistan, who says pain is pain wherever it sits, and Laila and Ayelet, a Palestinian mother and an Israeli sister, who turned loss into listening. The film then jumps to Doha, where Search for Common Ground's Israeli and Palestinian colleagues keep the space alive, and to Nairobi, where Palestinian staff find hope in each other. It ends on a call to see the people on the ground, which leads into the interlude and Chapter 5.

chapters.title: Imagine if…
chapters.line: A breather at the film's midpoint, after the hardest chapter. One stranger after another picks up the Imagine If phone under the Washington Square arch and says what they would tell the world. No interviews, light music, each voice its own short line.

chapters.title: On the ground
chapters.line: The film leaves the conference rooms and goes where conflict is real. Four short stories, each with a turn: in South Sudan people afraid to leave a camp walk to market again; in Sierra Leone a man who lost brothers in the war builds 10,000 election observers; in Syria a woman called a traitor gets an aid permit through; in Nairobi partners from war zones meet for the first time and name their small victories.

chapters.title: The next table
chapters.line: Who sits at the next table? First the children of Kërçova, taught side by side in two languages since the 1990s, kept in class even during the 2001 conflict, until the model became part of the national system. Then the leaders of Search for Common Ground in Doha: a CEO who says this kind of leadership is lonely, and a wall of answers from around the world that says it does not have to be, ending on a question every viewer can ask: what did I do to make the next generation's future possible?

chapters.title: Common ground at home
chapters.line: The film comes home to the United States. A street question in Dallas ("Who's your enemy?") opens a tour of Common Ground Gatherings in Austin, Orlando, Washington and New Orleans, where strangers who disagree share one table. Kalindi carries us to New York, where Bethany and her friend from the Chapter 1 picnic come back to talk about differences, then a year later postcards of peace pass from stranger to stranger, ending on a message that pulls into the finale.

chapters.title: Imagine if
chapters.line: The finale, back in Central Park. Strangers write down their wishes and let them go, a classical singer sings into a tin can, and the people we met in chapter 1 come back with what they hope for. It builds to Courtney's idea of "space" and ends on Alex: anybody, everybody, is good at something. The film's last minute (Courtney, "if you just remember the word space", and the hug) follows.

chapters.title: Ending
chapters.line: The film comes back to the park path and closes the space.

[00:00] We're good to go.
[00:02] Thank you.
[00:04] Ida, could you tell us about your work in Iran, France, and the most significant lesson you've learned?
[00:10] Yes. So I am an Iranian-French activist.
[00:14] I am the co-founder of We Are Iranian Students Association that works for the defense of Iranian students' rights.
[00:23] And I also work with Les Guerriers de la Paix in Paris that work with Israeli, Palestinian,
[00:31] but also the broader civil societies in different continents that work together towards peace, justice, and dignity.
[00:40] I think the most important lesson that I've learned those past four years is that you do not need to agree on everything to
[00:51] work together.
[00:55] Which has been something that is a groundbreaking, honestly, lesson given the binary narrative
[01:06] and the camps that we see in the polarization of our civil societies.
[01:12] The thing is that the more we are divided, the less we have power to put pressure on the decision-makers
[01:22] for them to take the concrete and necessary actions for the peace to prevail instead of destruction and chaos.
[01:31] And the more we are divided, the more we are distracted by our inner conflicts,
[01:37] the less we have power to actually put pressure on the people who benefit from our division,
[01:45] benefit from the conflicts, benefit from the armed industries.
[01:50] And this is the best way they have found to just weaken the power of civil societies
[01:58] who actually share exactly the same interests just regardless of where they live.
[02:07] The Iranian civil society, Palestinian, Israeli, Lebanese, French, American.
[02:14] You can take any civil society in the world, they are made of human beings who just want a dignified life
[02:21] and want to offer future generations something else than conflict, chaos, and death.
[02:27] So when we have those same, those shared interests, this is the ground to begin to work together
[02:38] without demanding that we agree on everything. We will not agree on everything.
[02:44] And we will not have justice. The world has not built itself through justice.
[02:51] The world has built itself through conflict and power balances that many, or I think all of them,
[03:02] all of those battles of powers ended up somewhere unjust.
[03:08] How we manage this as human beings and human societies is accountability.
[03:16] And this creates environments that are more or less, as much as we can, fair for people, not just.
[03:26] Justice would be giving back what people have lost, which is not possible.
[03:32] But creating an atmosphere in the future that can be more fair for a future generation,
[03:39] this is something that depends on accountability.
[03:42] So we need the civil society to be aware that they do not need to agree on everything to work together.
[03:48] So this collective power becomes something that we can use to put pressure then on decision makers.
[03:55] And they have their responsibility as well, because people who are here, they are taking immense risk
[04:02] appearing together, talking to each other. They are fighting against their intimate trauma.
[04:12] And they are all hurt. And they have so many reasons not to be here.
[04:17] And when they go back home, they have to face their community. They have to face their own inner disagreement.
[04:27] And they do all of this because they believe and they are building the ground for future decisions to be made.
[04:35] And if those decisions do not come, they will have done all those efforts for nothing.
[04:41] So it's the responsibility of decision makers also not just to upload them and be inspired by them,
[04:49] but also give them the means to have an agency to make this piece possible.
[04:55] It's not about liking each other. It's not about agreeing on everything with each other.
[05:04] We make peace with enemies. We don't make peace with friends.
[05:07] They have all understood this. And they know that they are working on this common future for common interests.
[05:17] And they need decision makers to honor this effort.
[05:21] I'm going to ask one last quick question because I want you to have two minutes.
[05:26] Could you maybe give us an example of something that has worked in Iran,
[05:32] maybe about the role of students or women, something specific to your work?
[05:39] What has worked in Iran?
[05:44] I think the non-violent movement, the women's life freedom movement,
[05:49] was the first movement that put the emancipation of the women at the core of the liberation of the whole society
[06:00] as a condition of the liberation of the civil society.
[06:05] That was the first time in history that happened.
[06:09] That happened in the most brutal Islamic fanatic criminal regime in the Middle East.
[06:18] And the opposition and the huge gap that was made obvious to the international community
[06:29] between the aspiration of the civil society, the non-violent principles and values,
[06:37] women's life freedom means equality, it means life under all its forms, it means environment, ecology, freedom,
[06:45] it means the end of all discrimination, religious discrimination against ethnicities.
[06:54] And I believe that they kept a non-violent identity that allowed this revolution
[07:03] to just go through all the borders and just beyond the Iranian borders
[07:10] and reach so many different countries and so many different also fights against discrimination
[07:20] and for feminism, for ecology.
[07:22] Every progressist movement somehow recognized itself in this huge wave.
[07:32] And I think also how the students organized so they could create content
[07:39] and they could share and make their values and aspirations known to the entire international community
[07:46] was really a key event that happened.
[07:49] The use of social media, the way that the art and the culture was at the center of it,
[07:56] because with art you can also reach so many different countries without talking the same language,
[08:05] but art is a very universal language.
[08:10] But what happened is exactly what we were talking about, the decision making didn't happen
[08:19] and they were left alone.
[08:21] So the civil societies can be very powerful, they can make the huge effort to talk to each other,
[08:28] to fight against their will, their traumas, against their fear, against their traumatic memories
[08:37] and reach out to each other, work together and then if the decision making does not happen,
[08:45] this is where we get stuck.
[08:48] So I think the non-violence, the culture, the values, the shared interests,
[08:55] the recognition that we do not need to agree with each other in order to work together
[09:03] and also the decision makers, they have to be part of it, they have to be in it with the civil societies,
[09:12] this dichotomy between civil society and decision makers is not working anymore.
[09:17] So we need action now and we need to do it collectively.

[00:04] in Northern Ireland, and the most significant lesson
[00:06] you've learned?
[00:08] In the city of my background, my dad
[00:11] was a politician in Ireland who dedicated a lot of his life
[00:15] to peace building.
[00:17] I grew up in Ireland on the border
[00:21] with a narrative that said that our independence was achieved
[00:24] through a violent revolution.
[00:26] So violence was the premise of my narrative.
[00:30] And everything that was bad was caused by the British
[00:33] and, by extension, caused by Protestants.
[00:37] Yet my dad was bringing the enemy to our home
[00:40] to talk about peace and peace building.
[00:44] And I had very animated rows with him about this.
[00:49] But I eventually realized that what he was doing
[00:52] was creating safe spaces for people
[00:55] who were willing to take the risk to have their story told.
[00:59] And that's the lens through which I
[01:02] started to look at the world.
[01:04] And that world, in the 70s, was a very dark world.
[01:10] Nothing like the scale of Palestine and the Israeli
[01:13] people are experiencing.
[01:16] But on a day-to-day basis, it was quite dark.
[01:21] So I started to work with the International Fund for Ireland
[01:24] in the field in very challenging environments
[01:28] where no one wanted us.
[01:31] Republicans didn't want us, Irish Republicans,
[01:34] because we were taking off the funding from the United States
[01:39] by putting it into peace building.
[01:42] The unionist community didn't want us
[01:43] because we were United Ireland people.
[01:46] The British and Irish governments sat off.
[01:49] So it was a very innovative, groundbreaking approach
[01:57] by giving agency to civic society
[02:01] and enabling civic society to have the resources to say
[02:07] to government, we want to negotiate with you now.
[02:11] And it began to take the oxygen away from the paramilitaries.
[02:16] So the role that civic society has played in Northern Ireland
[02:21] are really the unsung heroes of the peace process,
